fig10_1: Two side-by-side geometric diagrams illustrating the Chebyshev-Fourier link. The left diagram shows a unit semicircle with equally spaced angles theta sub j equals j times pi over N marked along the arc; dashed vertical lines project each point down to the horizontal axis, landing on Chebyshev points x sub j equals cosine theta sub j on the interval minus one to one, which visibly bunch together near the two endpoints plus and minus one and spread out near the centre. The right diagram depicts a Chebyshev polynomial T sub n of x as a cosine wave cosine of n theta drawn on a cylinder and viewed edge-on, conveying that the polynomial is a wrapped cosine seen through the cosine map.
fig10_2: Three panels demonstrating FFT-based Chebyshev differentiation of the function e to the power x times cosine of four x. The left panel plots the smooth oscillating function on minus one to one with the Chebyshev nodes marked as dots that cluster toward the endpoints. The centre panel overlays the FFT-computed derivative for N equal to sixteen on the exact derivative, the two curves coinciding. The right panel is a semilog plot of maximum error against N, where the error descends in a straight line, signalling exponential spectral convergence, until it flattens at machine precision near ten to the power minus fifteen around N equal to twenty-four.
tbl10_1: Table listing model time integrators for each PDE class, giving the semidiscrete form, typical schemes, and stability notes for wave, diffusion, and advection problems, showing that hyperbolic and advection equations use explicit schemes with a time step scaling like N to the minus two while diffusion prefers implicit schemes.
fig10_3: Waterfall plot of the one-dimensional wave equation solution u of x and t, with the spatial coordinate x from minus one to one along one horizontal axis and time t from zero to six stacked into the depth, the displacement shown as a sequence of offset profiles. The initial half-sine hump splits into two oppositely travelling pulses that bounce off the fixed ends at plus and minus one, inverting sign on each reflection, then cross and superpose to build a repeating standing-wave pattern, with no visible decay or spreading over the long integration.
fig10_4: Four contour or surface snapshots of a vibrating square drum membrane governed by the two-dimensional wave equation, at times zero, zero point three three, zero point six seven, and one. The first frame shows a single localised Gaussian bump placed off-centre; later frames show it expanding into a circular ring-shaped wavefront that strikes the fixed edges, reflects, and overlaps itself to form progressively more intricate interference patterns across the domain. The underlying tensor-product Chebyshev grid is denser near all four edges.
fig10_5: Combined view of the one-dimensional heat equation solution starting from two Gaussian hot spots of unequal height. The main panel is a space-time surface over x from minus one to one and increasing time, showing the warm regions smearing out and sinking in amplitude. Four inset line plots at times zero, zero point one, zero point three, and one capture successive snapshots in which the two bumps broaden, merge into one wider hump, and decay toward the flat zero steady state forced by the boundary conditions, illustrating irreversible diffusion.
fig10_6: Four contour or surface snapshots of the two-dimensional heat equation on a square at times zero, zero point zero five, zero point one five, and zero point five. The first frame shows a single concentrated Gaussian hot spot; the following frames show it diffusing outward symmetrically in all directions while its peak height steadily drops, smoothing toward the uniform zero steady state set by the fixed cold boundaries.
fig10_7: Four-panel two-by-two figure for the two-dimensional Poisson solver with a manufactured exact solution. Panel a shows a surface or contour of the exact solution over the square. Panel b shows the spectral numerical solution at N equal to thirty-two, indistinguishable by eye from panel a. Panel c maps the base-ten logarithm of the pointwise absolute error, which sits uniformly at machine precision throughout the interior. Panel d is a semilog plot of maximum error versus N, the error falling about four orders of magnitude for every four extra modes and levelling off at roughly ten to the power minus fifteen by N approximately sixteen, confirming exponential spectral convergence.
tbl10_2: Table reporting the maximum pointwise error of the two-dimensional Poisson spectral solver for grid sizes N from four to thirty-two, showing the error plunging from about six times ten to the minus two down to machine precision near ten to the minus fifteen by N equal to sixteen, after which it saturates.
tbl10_3: Table comparing the computational complexity of matrix-based versus FFT-based spectral differentiation for first and second one-dimensional derivatives and the two-dimensional Laplacian, showing the FFT approach reaching N log N or N squared log N cost where dense matrices need N squared, N cubed, or N to the fourth.
tbl10_4: Table summarising every PDE treated in the chapter alongside its section, grid type, time-stepping scheme, and key operation, spanning one- and two-dimensional wave, heat, Poisson, Helmholtz, and transport problems.
